title: Nature makes no leaps when past as well as present forms are included

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Nature makes no leaps when past as well as present forms are included

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: The rule that nature makes no leaps is not strictly true of living organisms alone, but if all past organisms are included it must be strictly true.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: This canon, if we look only to the present inhabitants of the world, is not strictly correct, but if we include all those of past times, it must by my theory be strictly true.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter VI, “Difficulties on Theory”; section “Natura non facit saltum.”. Scope: all organisms, living and extinct

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch06-16: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.40

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Selected lineages can test rates and apparent discontinuities. A strict statement covering every past organism cannot be confirmed, and missing intermediates are weak evidence of true leaps.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Define leap size in phenotypic or genetic character space and estimate transition magnitudes through densely sampled fossil and extant lineages. Repeated well-resolved discontinuities without intermediates would oppose strict gradualism.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
The complete history of all organisms is unrecoverable.

Sampling gaps can mimic leaps and flexible timescales can erase them.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Fossil occurrences and character matrices can test a proxy, continuity in well-sampled clades, with standard disparity methods. The stated claim is insulated by whatever is missing from the record, so every remaining gap is compatible both with saltation and with incompleteness. That is why discriminating power is low even though the raw databases are strong.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Measure morphological gaps between close relatives in well-sampled fossil clades and ask whether gaps shrink as specimens are added. Persistent large gaps after intense sampling would challenge a strict no-leap reading for those clades; gap-filling would support it only as a proxy, because the claim is about all past organisms, including those never preserved.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
The claim is defined over all past organisms, most of which were never preserved, so residual gaps do not refute it.

'Strictly true' has no tolerance for a single saltation, which cannot be audited.

Sampling and the Signor-Lipps effect manufacture apparent leaps.
